name: Adam Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play guitar for a busy small theatre, record chord guides and teach three older beginners. My music degree and twenty-five years on paid stages help me follow an actor who takes a line slowly. I like hearing a beginner's first clean chord more than any new piece of kit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that mix work for your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner works regular hours at a pharmacy and our children are grown. We own our flat, have eight months of expenses saved and my pay is high for this job. Several theatres and teaching centres are nearby, though an open chair still needs a paid posting. I use AI now and then to draft set lists, then check them with the stage manager.

say: I'd welcome **quicker set lists** with paid rehearsals written beside shows.
I'd say a **guitar player** still listens to an actor on stage.
think: Our **eight-month reserve** and partner wage cover a shifted performance.
The **theatre and lessons** should keep paying in mild AI.
do: Confirm **six paid shows** and three pupils; request written cancellation pay.
Check **AI set lists** against signed stage sheets and save twenty percent of an extra cleared festival fee after essentials.
feel: I feel **calm** while booked shows and household pay remain secure.
S0.quote: A guitar still needs a player listening to the actor on stage.
fieldNote: His **high musician pay** and eight-month reserve absorb one moved performance while his partner earns regular wages.
Occasional **AI set-list drafting** is existing use, checked with the stage manager.

steps.text: Confirm six paid shows and three pupils; request written cancellation fee
Check AI lists against stage sheet; save 20% of extra cleared festival fee after flat charges/food/repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre a quicker set list helps if it keeps the paid rehearsal beside each show. A guitar still needs a player listening to the actor on stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight months saved and my partner's steady pay can carry a shifted performance. I expect the theatre and three lessons to keep paying in this mild picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm six paid shows and three pupil slots, then ask for a written cancellation fee. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep checking occasional AI set lists against the signed stage sheet and save twenty percent of an extra cleared festival fee after flat charges, food and string repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work we have. A changed date would need paperwork, not a household crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the outdoor show moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A storm moved one outdoor performance last year. The contract paid the rehearsal, but the show fee took another month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes into the set-list draft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A set-list draft needs titles and timings, not cast recordings. I check the page with the stage manager before sharing it.

say: I'd ask which **paid chord guides** new software may replace.
I'd seek **written rates** for live playing and revisions before another season.
think: Guides provide **one fifth** of my own pay.
Our **eight-month reserve** and nearby venues give search time, not replacement income.
do: Compare **ten guide invoices** and request a paid engineer demonstration outside booked shows.
Test **AI timing checker** after paid demo outside paid shows, using owned nameless track, theatre-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage.
Compare **chord changes by ear**; stop errors or leakage and require written pupil consent for other audio.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing regular guide fees.
S1.quote: A faster edit helps my time, but it does not make a client order a guide.
fieldNote: The **new AI trial** requires paid engineer instruction outside show hours and commercially permitted private audio.
He **checks suggestions manually** and stops for wrong chords or leakage.

steps.text: Compare ten guide invoices and request paid engineer demo outside booked shows
Test after paid demo outside shows: owned nameless track, funded paid-use licence/local storage
Listen to changed chords; stop errors/leakage; require pupil consent for other audio

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the theatre how many paid chord-guide orders its new software may replace. I'd ask for the live playing and revision rates in writing before the next season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chord guides bring about one fifth of my own pay. Fewer orders would matter, but eight months saved and several local venues give me room to find other paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten chord-guide invoices with the new order list and ask a trusted engineer for a paid demonstration of the theatre's new AI timing checker. In the first year I'll test only a nameless track I own under a theatre-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage, outside paid show hours; I'll compare each suggestion by ear and stop for shifted chords or file leakage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic drop in guide fees. A faster edit helps my time, but it does not make a client order a guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the checker demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre must pay the engineer and licence without taking one of my paid show hours. If it won't, I'll keep my original track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test on a pupil's audio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I won't upload a pupil's playing for a trial. Another person's audio needs written permission and a storage rule first.

think: I expect **one-fifth pay** from guides to end in 2028.

do: Total **guide income**, request signed theatre calls and actual pension estimate before stopping work.
Seek **posted guitar-tutor work** after live cuts only if degree/teaching qualify, written net after travel replaces losses and bus fits.
Keep **theatre and pupils** until a suitable signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected guide loss with time to search.
S2.quote: Eight months saved cannot tell me what retirement would pay monthly.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 guide loss** comes before 2031 playing robots; live cuts remain conditional.

steps.text: Total guide income; request signed theatre calls and actual pension estimate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cast that thinking AGI by 2028 could make chord guides before a robot plays guitar. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I want signed live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to stop in 2028 and take a fifth of my pay. The live shows might thin later, but I cannot call that a lost wage while this season is booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total guide income, ask for signed paid theatre calls and request an actual pension estimate before discussing a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid guitar-tutor role only if my music degree and teaching experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus suits its hours; I'll keep the theatre and three pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected fifth of my own pay disappearing. Eight months saved and several local employers give time to look; I would be more upset if live work collapsed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a tutor role available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No centre has offered a tutor role. I would read a current paid posting and its requirements before counting that wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop work at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen an actual pension amount. Eight months saved cannot tell me what retirement would pay monthly.

say: I'd seek **paid guitar setup training** during the five-year warning.
I'd put **playing robots** around 2034 after guide changes.
think: Ordinary software may cut **chord guides before 2031**, ahead of playing robots.
I need **recognized supervised training** for neck and electrical work.
do: Take **recognised guitar-setup training** only with funded paid place/tools, matched displaced show wages, preserved pupil lessons and qualified supervision.
Seek **posted setup work** after 2031 guide/show cuts only if certificate qualifies, written net after travel replaces losses and buses fit.
Keep **theatre and pupils** until signed offer; perform neck/electrical checks under technician until signed approval.
feel: I feel **anxious** until paid training and a real job exist.
S3.quote: A guitar-setup certificate no local repair shop accepts would not replace a cancelled show.
fieldNote: The **six-month course** needs prior shop recognition, funded tuition/tools, an actual paid place and protected show wages.
The **repair role** requires posted paid work, certificate fit, replacement net after travel and supervised safety checks.

steps.text: Confirm recognition before funded paid guitar-setup place/tools; protect show wages/pupil slots and qualified supervision
Work under qualified technician on neck/electrical checks until signed safety approval
Seek posted setup-assistant job after guide/show cuts if certificate qualifies and buses fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre that five years to AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn paid guitar setup work, adjusting strings and the guitar neck, at a repair shop. Playing robots follow around 2034, after software changes chord guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cheapen the guides before 2031. I can change strings, but I have not been trained to adjust a neck under tension or sell a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll ask nearby repair shops whether they recognize the six-month guitar-setup certificate before enrolling. I'll take an actual paid apprentice place only if the shop funds tuition and tools, its wages match any paid theatre calls the training displaces, paid pupil slots remain intact, and a qualified technician supervises neck and electrical checks. In the first year after 2031, if guide orders stop and paid shows fall, I'll seek a posted paid setup-assistant role only if the certificate qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses work after shifts; I'll keep theatre and pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious until both the apprentice place and a real job pay. A guitar-setup certificate no local repair shop accepts would not replace a cancelled show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work alone after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not adjust a tense neck or check live electronics by myself after a course. The technician must sign the first safety checks before I work alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tuition is covered but wages fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop pays tuition but not enough wages, I'll keep my paid shows and ask about a later intake. A free course can still cost us fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us read pension figures and written theatre calls. Guitar-playing robots follow around 2039, but a birthday does not pay a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still enjoy paid shows and beginner lessons. Eight months saved and our flat help, but I will not assume a pension amount before seeing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid-call plan, then save twenty percent of each extra cleared festival fee after flat charges, food and guitar repairs toward twelve months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid shows and pupils while booked; if live pay falls and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted guitar-tutor role only if my degree and teaching qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and bus times fit, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about pay that far away while current bookings and eight months saved are sound. I will slow down only when the real pension and paid dates cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No extra festival set means no transfer from that source. I will not move food money to reach twelve months on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen pension figures yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not received my pension figures yet. I will read the statement with my partner before dropping a paid show.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid chord guides could end before another teaching post opens. Signed theatre calls, actual pension figures and a posted qualified tutor role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first repaired guitar neck after a course. A guitar-setup certificate cannot stop a string snapping near a student's hand.

headlineQuote: A guitar-setup certificate cannot stop a string snapping near a student's hand.
portrait: Adam is a **58-year-old experienced guitarist** with a music degree, partner and grown children.
His **higher pay**, eight-month reserve and many nearby venues give time to respond to guide losses.
He uses **AI occasionally** for set lists and tests a new timing checker only with paid instruction and owned audio.
He seeks **funded paid guitar-setup training** only with employer recognition, protected wages and supervised safety checks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a fifth of Adam's pay from chord guides.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying tutoring with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
